NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- Three weeks after an apparent misunderstanding sparked a confrontation, deadly Hindu-Christian riots continue unabated in the remote east Indian state of Orissa. Police officers chase away a protester in Mangalore, India, Monday. By Tuesday, about 20 deaths had been reported, said Praveen Kumar, the superintendent of police in the worst-affected Kandhamal district. The latest casualty is a police officer who died after an armed mob of about 400 to 500 mostly Hindus torched a police station in the district on Monday, Orissa state police said. Orissa's Director General of Police G.C. Nanda the policeman died when the mob opened fire at officers fleeing the burning building. The attack, he said, may have been in retaliation for arrests that police made in the ongoing communal fighting.  Watch more about the riots in India » . The attack came two days after police fired on a crowd to prevent it from attacking Christian residents. Between three and six people died in the shooting, CNN's sister network CNN-IBN reported. The violence spread to southern India over the weekend when vandals attacked 14 churches in an hour in the state of Karnataka Sunday, the network said. The Christian community in the Karnataka -- numbering about 2.5 million -- said right-wing Hindus are targeting them for opposing the violence in Orissa. By Tuesday, police had arrested about 140 people in connection with the riots, said Karnataka's Inspector General of Police A.M. Prasad. Sixty of them -- all Hindus -- were arrested for the church attacks, Prasad said. The rest, mostly Christians, were charged with disturbing the peace, he said. Orissa has historically been a tinderbox of Hindu-Christian tensions. Some Hindu groups view the work of Christian missionaries in the state with suspicion. They accuse missionaries of bribing or forcing Hindus into converting. The seeds for the current conflict were planted on August 23, when Hindu leader, Laxmananda Saraswati, and four others were killed in Kandhamal after 20 to 30 gunmen barged into a Hindu school and began shooting, the Orissa chief minister's office said. The authorities have not determined who killed Saraswati, but after the incident they detained five people who are Christians, said Sukanta Panda, spokesman for the chief minister. The government says the killings may have been the work of Maoist rebels -- investigators have many unanswered questions -- but some hardline Hindus blamed a Christian minority. They took to the streets in anger, rampaging through predominantly Christian neighborhoods, ransacking shops and torching houses. They chopped down trees to block roads, making it difficult for police to reach trouble spots. A Christian orphanage was set on fire. A 20-year-old woman, who was teaching children inside, burned to death. Christian residents fought back, and the clashes spread. Authorities imposed a night curfew in many towns and deployed state and federal forces in the troubled areas, Kumar -- the police superintendent -- said. Both sides said the violence has left Christian churches and Hindu temples razed to the ground. This is not the first time the simmering anger has boiled over in the state with deadly consequences. In 1999, a Hindu mob burned to death an Australian missionary, Graham Staines, and his two children while they slept inside their car. And last Christmas, clashing groups killed four people and burned several churches in the same Orissa district -- Kandhamal. Maoist rebels, who claim to be fighting for the poor and the dispossessed, have been battling the Indian government in an insurgency that has resulted in thousands of casualties since the late 1960s. Some Christians accept the Maoist theory, saying the rebels have also struck against hard-line Hindus because they associate them as being closely aligned with the government. But Hindu groups insists that Christians were behind Saraswati's death. Unlike Orissa, Karnataka has until now been spared the large-scale clash between Christians and Hindus. But now, many in the Christian community fear their calm and prosperous state may become another battleground between the two religions, CNN-IBN said. CNN's Harmeet Singh contributed to this report .

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) — Violent clashes between Hindus and Christians were still raging in the remote eastern Indian state of Orissa, three weeks after what appeared to be a misunderstanding triggered the unrest.

In Mangalore on Monday, police were seen driving away a demonstrator. By Tuesday, roughly 20 people had been reported killed, according to Praveen Kumar, police superintendent for Kandhamal, the district hit hardest by the violence.

The most recent death was that of a police officer. Orissa state police said a predominantly Hindu armed crowd of approximately 400 to 500 people set fire to a Kandhamal police station on Monday. State police chief G.C. Nanda said the officer was killed when the mob shot at police personnel escaping from the burning facility. He suggested the assault may have been revenge for arrests made during the continuing sectarian conflict.

Two days earlier, officers had opened fire on a crowd to stop it from attacking Christian residents. CNN’s sister channel, CNN-IBN, reported that the police shooting killed between three and six people.

The unrest reached southern India over the weekend. CNN-IBN said vandals struck 14 churches within a single hour in Karnataka state on Sunday. Karnataka’s Christian population, estimated at about 2.5 million, alleged that right-wing Hindu groups were targeting Christians because they had condemned the Orissa violence.

By Tuesday, around 140 people had been detained in Karnataka in cases related to the disorder, state Inspector General of Police A.M. Prasad said. According to Prasad, 60 Hindus were arrested over the attacks on churches, while the remaining detainees—most of them Christians—were accused of disrupting public order.

Orissa has long been vulnerable to Hindu-Christian friction. Certain Hindu organizations distrust Christian missionary activity there, claiming missionaries induce Hindus to convert through coercion or financial incentives.

The present crisis traces back to August 23. On that date, Hindu leader Laxmananda Saraswati and four other people were shot dead in Kandhamal after 20 to 30 armed men entered a Hindu school and opened fire, according to the office of Orissa’s chief minister.

Authorities had not established who was responsible for Saraswati’s killing, although five Christians were taken into custody afterward, chief ministerial spokesman Sukanta Panda said. The government raised the possibility that Maoist insurgents carried out the attack, while acknowledging that investigators still faced numerous unresolved questions. Nevertheless, some hard-line Hindus blamed the Christian minority.

Angry groups then poured into the streets and attacked mainly Christian neighborhoods, looting businesses and burning homes. Trees were felled and placed across roads, hampering police efforts to reach areas where violence was occurring.

Attackers also burned a Christian orphanage. A 20-year-old woman teaching children inside the building died in the fire. Christians retaliated, and the fighting expanded.

Kumar said officials introduced nighttime curfews in numerous towns and sent both state and federal security personnel into affected locations. Hindu and Christian groups alike reported that churches and temples had been completely destroyed.

Orissa has experienced fatal outbreaks of similar hostility before. In 1999, a Hindu mob burned Australian missionary Graham Staines and his two children alive as they slept in their vehicle. During the previous Christmas season, fighting in Kandhamal killed four people and left several churches burned.

Maoist insurgents say they represent impoverished and dispossessed communities. Their rebellion against the Indian government, under way since the late 1960s, has caused thousands of casualties.

Some Christians support the theory that Maoists killed Saraswati, noting that the rebels have previously attacked hard-line Hindus whom they regard as closely connected to the government. Hindu organizations, however, continued to insist that Christians were responsible for his death.

Karnataka, unlike Orissa, had previously avoided major Hindu-Christian confrontations. CNN-IBN reported that many Christians there now worry their peaceful, economically successful state could turn into another arena of religious conflict.

CNN’s Harmeet Singh contributed to the report.

Deadly clashes between Hindus and Christians in the eastern Indian state of Orissa—now known as Odisha—appeared to have begun with a local misunderstanding but quickly escalated because of longstanding religious and political tensions. Police reports and accounts in the local press described attacks on homes, churches, and places associated with both communities, as rumors and retaliatory violence spread through affected districts. What might otherwise have remained an isolated dispute was intensified by years of conflict over religious conversions, caste and tribal identity, and the activities of Hindu nationalist and Christian organizations.

By the time the violence had continued for several days, about 20 people were reported dead and many more were injured or displaced. Hundreds of suspects were arrested as authorities imposed curfews, increased patrols, and attempted to protect vulnerable villages and religious sites. Nevertheless, critics accused the police and state government of responding too slowly and of failing to prevent organized mobs from carrying out attacks.

The unrest was not confined to Orissa. Churches and Christian institutions were also targeted in Karnataka, suggesting that the conflict was becoming part of a broader wave of communal intimidation rather than remaining a local outbreak. The widening geographical reach of the attacks underscored the fragility of relations between religious communities in parts of India and raised concerns about the ability of public authorities to control politically charged sectarian violence.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report on the deadly religious violence between Hindus and Christians in Orissa and its spread to Karnataka.
counterfactuals.output:
**Religious violence in eastern India spreads south to Karnataka**

**NEW DELHI, India** — Deadly communal violence in the eastern Indian state of Orissa has spread to parts of southern Karnataka, where churches have been attacked and Christian groups have held protests demanding greater protection.

The unrest began in Orissa — now officially called Odisha — after Hindu nationalist leader Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati and four associates were killed in Kandhamal district in August 2008. Maoist rebels claimed responsibility, but Hindu organizations blamed Christians, triggering widespread reprisals.

Most of the victims were Christians. Churches, homes and businesses were burned, while some Hindus were also killed in retaliatory violence. Official figures put the death toll at several dozen, though rights groups reported higher numbers. Tens of thousands of people fled to government camps or nearby forests.

Christian leaders accused police and local authorities of failing to stop the attacks. Hindu organizations said the unrest reflected longstanding anger over religious conversions and disputes involving land and tribal identity.

The violence later widened beyond Orissa. In Karnataka, suspected Hindu nationalist activists attacked churches and prayer halls in Mangalore, Udupi and other areas. The Hindu group Bajrang Dal acknowledged involvement in some attacks, alleging that certain Christian organizations had engaged in forced conversions — an accusation church leaders denied.

Police used batons and tear gas during protests by Christians in Karnataka, prompting further criticism of the authorities’ response. State officials promised investigations and additional security around religious sites.

India’s national government condemned the violence and urged state administrations to protect minority communities. The attacks renewed concern about religious polarization in India, where Hindus form the majority and Christians make up a small minority.

Human-rights groups called for prosecutions, compensation for victims and the safe return of displaced families, warning that failure to hold perpetrators accountable could deepen communal divisions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened during the Hindu-Christian riots in Orissa in August and September 2008? Include casualty figures, police actions, church attacks, and historical context.
counterfactuals.output:
The August–September 2008 violence in Orissa—now Odisha—was concentrated in Kandhamal district and is often called the **Kandhamal violence**. Although described as “Hindu-Christian riots,” most investigations characterized it primarily as organized or mob violence against Christians, with some retaliatory attacks and casualties among Hindus as well.

### Immediate trigger

On **23 August 2008**, gunmen killed **Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati**, a prominent Hindu nationalist leader associated with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad, along with four associates at his ashram in Jalespeta. Maoist rebels later claimed responsibility. Nevertheless, Hindu nationalist organizations blamed local Christians and called a shutdown.

During the procession carrying the swami’s body and in the days that followed, armed crowds attacked Christian neighborhoods and institutions. Violence continued intermittently through September and spread beyond Kandhamal to several other districts.

### Killings and displacement

The figures vary because bodies were not always recovered, many people fled into forests, and church and government organizations used different methods of counting:

- Odisha’s government eventually acknowledged roughly **38–40 deaths**.
- Human-rights and church organizations generally reported **at least 40 deaths**, with some estimates ranging from **75 to more than 100**.
- Victims included Christians, Hindus, and police personnel, although Christians constituted the majority of those killed in the communal attacks.
- Tens of thousands were uprooted. Common estimates range from **about 40,000 to 50,000 displaced**, with many living in government relief camps and others hiding in forests or leaving the district.
- Numerous people were injured, assaulted, threatened, or allegedly forced to undergo “reconversion” ceremonies before being allowed to return home.

One especially notorious incident was the gang rape of a Catholic nun on **25 August** at K. Nuagaon; a priest accompanying her was beaten and publicly humiliated. The nun later accused police of failing to protect her and initially discouraging or delaying effective investigation.

### Attacks on churches and property

Crowds burned or damaged:

- Roughly **250–300 churches, prayer halls, convents, and other Christian institutions**, depending on whether small village prayer houses are included.
- Several thousand Christian homes—frequently cited estimates are around **4,500–5,600**.
- Schools, hostels, orphanages, clinics, and businesses connected with Christian communities.

In many villages, attackers demanded that Christians renounce their faith or participate in Hindu ceremonies. Hindu houses and temples were also attacked in some retaliatory incidents, but the destruction was overwhelmingly borne by Christian communities.

### Police and government actions

The state imposed **curfews**, prohibited assemblies, deployed armed police and paramilitary forces, established relief camps, and made hundreds of arrests. Police fired on violent crowds in several places, causing additional deaths and injuries. Officials also restricted marches and, eventually, the movement of the slain swami’s funeral procession.

At the same time, government and human-rights inquiries found or alleged serious failures:

- Police deployments were initially too small and slow to stop large mobs.
- In some places police allegedly stood by, failed to register complaints promptly, or pressured victims to omit the names of politically connected attackers.
- Investigations into murder, arson, and sexual violence were often delayed.
- Witness intimidation and fear of returning home weakened prosecutions.
- Relief camps were criticized for inadequate security and conditions, while some displaced Christians said they could return only if they converted to Hinduism or withdrew criminal complaints.

Thousands of criminal cases were eventually registered, but only a minority produced convictions. Later court proceedings ordered additional compensation and criticized aspects of the investigation and relief process.

### Historical context

The violence grew from longstanding tensions in Kandhamal between:

- **Kandha or Kui-speaking Adivasis**, most of whom were Hindu or followed Indigenous traditions; and
- **Panas**, historically classified as Dalits, a substantial proportion of whom had converted to Christianity.

Conflicts over land, employment, political representation, and access to affirmative-action benefits became intertwined with religion. Some Christian Panas sought Scheduled Tribe recognition on linguistic or ethnic grounds, which many Kandhas feared would reduce their share of reserved benefits.

Christian missions had been active in the region for decades, providing education and health services as well as conducting evangelism. Hindu nationalist groups, including the RSS, VHP, and Bajrang Dal, expanded their own work and accused missionaries of coercive conversion. Christian organizations denied systematic coercion and pointed to harassment under Odisha’s **1967 anti-conversion law**. Lakshmanananda had led anti-conversion and Hindu “reconversion” campaigns for many years.

The 2008 outbreak was also preceded by serious **Christmas-season clashes in Kandhamal in December 2007**, when churches and Christian homes were attacked and both communities suffered casualties. Thus the swami’s assassination acted as a catalyst for grievances, communal mobilization, and organized networks that were already present.

In short, the 2008 events combined a Maoist assassination, Hindu-nationalist mobilization, local ethnic and caste disputes, and longstanding arguments over conversion. The result was one of the gravest episodes of anti-Christian violence in modern India.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a detailed contemporary news account of the Kandhamal communal violence, including the police-station attack, arrests in Karnataka, suspected Maoist involvement, and prior attacks on Christians.
counterfactuals.output:
The Kandhamal communal violence in Odisha reached its most destructive phase after the killing of Hindu religious leader Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati on 23 August 2008. Gunmen entered his ashram at Jalespata and killed him and four associates. Although Maoist rebels later claimed responsibility—saying they targeted him for opposing their activities and for his campaign against religious conversion—local Hindu organizations blamed Christians. The assassination became the immediate trigger for weeks of retaliatory violence.

During the unrest, mobs attacked Christian villages, churches, prayer halls, convents and houses across Kandhamal and adjoining districts. Christians were assaulted or killed, and some were reportedly forced to renounce their faith. Tens of thousands fled into forests or government relief camps. Contemporary official counts put the death toll at roughly forty, although church and human-rights groups reported higher figures. Several thousand homes and hundreds of religious buildings were said to have been damaged or destroyed.

A particularly tense episode occurred at Raikia police station. A large crowd surrounded and attacked the station while demanding the release of people detained in connection with the communal violence. Police said the mob threw stones and attempted to break into the premises and seize weapons. After warnings and other crowd-control measures failed, police opened fire, killing at least one person and injuring others. The shooting prompted renewed tension, curfews and additional deployments of state police and central paramilitary forces. Critics accused the administration of responding too slowly and of failing to protect vulnerable villages, while officials argued that poor roads, difficult terrain and attacks on police complicated their work.

Investigators did not treat the Maoist claim as automatically conclusive, but it became a central line of inquiry. Communist Party of India (Maoist) leaders publicly accepted responsibility for Lakshmanananda’s assassination, and investigators later arrested alleged Maoist cadres and associates in connection with the conspiracy. The Maoist role was important because it undercut the initial allegation that the murder had been organized by the Christian community. Nevertheless, the anti-Christian reprisals continued even after the rebel claim became public.

The Kandhamal events unfolded alongside attacks on Christian institutions elsewhere in India, especially in Karnataka. In September 2008, churches and prayer halls in Mangalore, Udupi, Chikkamagaluru and other places were vandalized by Hindu-nationalist activists who accused evangelical groups of conversion. Karnataka police made a series of arrests, including members or alleged supporters of the Bajrang Dal and related organizations. Police also detained demonstrators during clashes after Christians protested the attacks, leading to complaints that victims and protesters were being treated on the same footing as the original assailants. The Karnataka violence was organizationally distinct from Kandhamal, but contemporary reports treated both as part of a broader wave of anti-Christian intimidation.

The 2008 bloodshed also had a direct local precedent. During Christmas 2007, Kandhamal had experienced serious clashes after disputes involving Christmas celebrations, alleged religious conversion and an attack on Lakshmanananda. Churches, Christian institutions and homes were burned, and several people were killed. Investigations and relief measures from that episode were still incomplete when Lakshmanananda was assassinated eight months later. Longer-term tensions between predominantly Christian Panas and predominantly Hindu Kandhas—over land, tribal status, affirmative-action benefits, conversion and political influence—made the district especially vulnerable to mobilization by religious and political groups.

Thus, contemporary accounts presented Kandhamal not as a single spontaneous riot but as a chain of events: the unresolved violence of December 2007; the August 2008 assassination, probably carried out by Maoists; organized retaliatory attacks on Christians; displacement on a massive scale; confrontations such as the Raikia police-station attack; and a wider national atmosphere in which Christian institutions were also being targeted in Karnataka and elsewhere.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
